When you describe something as sexist, you are saying that it reflects, expresses, or causes unfair treatment of a person — or an entire group of people — based solely on their sex or gender.

The underlying assumption driving anything "sexist" is this: one sex is naturally better, more capable, more important, or more suited for certain roles than the other. When that assumption shapes someone's words, actions, decisions, or thinking, the result is something sexist.

The adjective can describe a wide range of things:

  • A remark or joke — "Women are terrible drivers."
  • An attitude or belief — Assuming that men are naturally better leaders.
  • A behavior — Interrupting a woman in a meeting but patiently listening to men.
  • A decision or policy — Paying a woman less than a male colleague doing the same job.
  • A question — Asking a female job applicant, "Do you plan to have children?" but never asking men the same.
  • A system or institution — A workplace culture where women are routinely overlooked for promotions.
  • Language — Using "mankind" to mean "all people," which erases women from the picture.

While "sexist" can technically describe unfair treatment directed at any gender, it most commonly — and historically — refers to bias and discrimination against women. This is because for most of recorded history, societies were structured in ways that placed men above women in power, rights, and opportunity.

That said, men can also be targets of sexist thinking — for example, the assumption that men are emotionally weak for crying, or that fathers are naturally less capable of caring for children than mothers. These too are sexist, because they enforce a rigid, unfair idea of what each sex is "supposed" to be like.

Sexist attitudes and actions exist on a wide spectrum.

Overt sexism is open and undisguised. It is easy to spot:

  • "Women don't belong in science."
  • Refusing to hire women for certain jobs simply because they are women.

Subtle sexism is harder to see, but it is just as real. It often comes in the form of small, everyday moments — sometimes called microaggressions:

  • A man explaining something to a woman in an unnecessarily simple way, assuming she won't understand — even when she is an expert in that very topic (this is so common it has its own name: mansplaining).
  • Automatically assuming the nurse is a woman and the doctor is a man.
  • Praising a woman for being "surprisingly assertive" — which implies that assertiveness is unusual or unexpected in women.

These small moments might seem harmless in isolation, but over time, they add up and reinforce the idea that one sex is less capable or less deserving of respect.
Benevolent sexism — the "positive" kind that is still harmful

This is one of the most important and misunderstood aspects of sexism, so it deserves its own explanation.

Not all sexism looks like hatred or hostility. Some sexism comes dressed up as kindness, protection, or compliments. This is called benevolent sexism, and it is still sexist because it still treats women as a category that is fundamentally different from, and weaker or less capable than, men.

Examples:

  • "Women are too gentle and emotional for the rough world of business." (said as if it is a compliment to women's sensitivity)
  • "Men should always protect women." (sounds chivalrous, but implies women are fragile and helpless)
  • "Women are naturally better at nurturing children." (sounds positive, but locks women into a narrow role)

Why is this sexist if it sounds nice? Because it still relies on the assumption that women as a whole share certain traits that make them suited for some things and unsuited for others — which denies women their individuality and limits their freedom and choices.

A crucial point: something can be sexist even when no harm was intended.

A person can hold sexist beliefs without being aware of it. These are called unconscious biases — assumptions that have been absorbed so gradually, through upbringing, media, and culture, that the person never stops to question them.

For example, a manager might genuinely believe he is fair and objective, yet consistently rate women's work more critically than men's doing identical work. He may not intend to discriminate, but the outcome is still sexist.

This is why the word "sexist" describes the nature of an action, attitude, or statement — not necessarily a verdict on whether the person is a bad person. You can call a remark sexist without saying the person who made it is irredeemably evil. It simply means: this remark carries an unfair assumption about someone's sex.

Beyond individual actions, "sexist" can also describe entire systems, structures, or institutions that consistently disadvantage one sex.

When a country's laws historically forbade women from voting, owning property, or working in certain professions — that entire legal system was sexist. When a company's internal culture, promotion patterns, and pay scales consistently favor men over equally qualified women — that company has systemic sexist practices, even if no single person is consciously discriminating.

This is important because systemic sexism can persist even after the people within that system have all personally rejected sexist beliefs, simply because the old, biased rules and habits were never changed.
How to recognize if something is sexist

Ask yourself: Would this be said, done, or decided differently if the person's sex were different?

  • Would the manager have interrupted a male employee the same way?
  • Would the interviewer have asked a male candidate whether he plans to have children?
  • Would the advertisement have shown a man cleaning the house and caring for children, or only a woman?

If the answer is no — if the person's sex is the reason for the different treatment — that is what makes it sexist.

Sexist describes anything — a word, a joke, an attitude, a behavior, a policy, or a system — that treats a person unfairly, dismissively, or in a limiting way because of their sex or gender. It is rooted in the assumption that the sexes are unequal in worth, ability, or the roles they should occupy. It can be blatant or subtle, hostile or seemingly kind, intentional or completely unconscious. What unites all of it is the same thing: a person is being judged, limited, or harmed not for who they are as an individual, but simply because of the sex they were born into.
